title: Week 16 · Lesson 40: Pain & Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Nonopioid Analgesics, NSAIDs & Opioid Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 16 — Lesson 40: Pain & Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Nonopioid Analgesics, NSAIDs & Opioid Safety

FNP-level goal: Build a diagnosis-first, function-centered pain plan that uses nonopioid options safely, recognizes medication harms, and treats opioid decisions as an ongoing clinical responsibility rather than a refill task.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic, and centrally amplified pain before selecting medication.
  • Compare acetaminophen, topical/oral NSAIDs, adjuvant analgesics, and opioids by mechanism, benefit, and harm.
  • Recognize renal, cardiovascular, GI, hepatic, bleeding, sedation, and fall-risk medication concerns.
  • Apply a function-centered approach to acute, subacute, and chronic pain.
  • Use opioid risk assessment, monitoring, naloxone counseling, and nonjudgmental reassessment appropriately.
  • Identify pain presentations requiring urgent evaluation rather than analgesic escalation.

Part 1 — Pain Is a Signal, a Disease Process, and Sometimes an Emergency

Pain treatment begins with a working diagnosis. Acute pain after a sprain differs from inflammatory arthritis, radicular pain, fracture, septic joint, renal colic, ischemia, abdominal catastrophe, malignancy-related pain, and chronic centralized pain. Medication should support the diagnostic and functional plan; it must not conceal deterioration.

First ask: Is there a red flag? Trauma with deformity, fever with a hot swollen joint, new neurologic deficit, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, severe unremitting pain, limb ischemia, chest pain, abdominal rigidity, or concern for infection/compartment syndrome changes disposition immediately.

Part 2 — Mechanism Guides Medication Choice

Nociceptive pain arises from tissue injury or mechanical stress. Inflammatory pain involves inflammatory mediators and may respond differently from purely mechanical pain. Neuropathic pain reflects lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and is often described as burning, electric, shooting, or allodynic. Central sensitization can amplify pain and disability beyond ongoing peripheral tissue injury.

One medication class will not appropriately treat every mechanism. A plan may include rehabilitation, sleep support, behavioral strategies, weight-bearing or strengthening work when appropriate, topical/local options, and medication selected for a defined mechanism.

Part 3 — Function Is the Outcome, Not a Perfect Pain Score

For subacute or chronic pain, define a functional goal that matters to the patient: walking, sleeping, caring for a child, working a shift, participating in physical therapy, or tolerating a medical procedure. A numeric pain score is useful only in context.

Before starting a higher-risk medication, establish what benefit would justify continuing it, what adverse effects would stop it, how soon it will be reassessed, and what nonpharmacologic support is feasible. “Pain is still 8/10” is not enough information to justify automatic escalation.

Part 4 — Acetaminophen: Common Does Not Mean Risk-Free

Acetaminophen is often used for acute musculoskeletal pain, fever, and selected chronic pain contexts. Its major safety concern is dose-related liver injury. The FNP must count all sources: prescription combination products, OTC cold/flu products, sleep aids, and multiple pain medicines may contain acetaminophen.

Assess liver disease, alcohol use, nutritional status, other hepatotoxic medications, and the total daily amount. Patient education should use the exact product and label, not a vague instruction to “take Tylenol as needed.”

Part 5 — NSAIDs: Helpful Anti-Inflammatory Drugs With Systemic Tradeoffs

NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and inflammation. Topical NSAIDs may provide a favorable option for selected localized musculoskeletal conditions because systemic exposure is lower than with oral therapy. Oral NSAIDs may be appropriate for selected patients, but the medication choice is inseparable from kidney function, blood pressure, heart failure, cardiovascular disease, GI history, bleeding risk, pregnancy status, and concurrent drugs.

Do not prescribe oral NSAIDs as though they are benign short courses. A “few days” can still matter in a patient with CKD, volume depletion, heart failure, anticoagulation, prior ulcer, older age, or combined RAAS-blocking and diuretic therapy.

Part 6 — The NSAID Kidney and Heart-Failure Problem

Prostaglandins help maintain renal perfusion in vulnerable states. NSAID exposure can worsen kidney perfusion and sodium/water retention, particularly in volume depletion or in patients taking a diuretic plus an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI. This can contribute to acute kidney injury, higher blood pressure, edema, or heart-failure decompensation.

Ask about new weight gain, edema, lower urine output, dizziness, vomiting/diarrhea, home blood pressures, and all pain products—not only the medication you are about to prescribe.

Part 7 — GI and Bleeding Risk Are Part of NSAID Prescribing

NSAIDs can increase ulcer and GI-bleeding risk. The risk is higher with prior ulcer/GI bleed, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, alcohol exposure, multiple NSAID products, and older age. Gastroprotection may be clinically appropriate in some situations, but it is not permission to ignore an unsafe overall risk profile.

Black stools, hematemesis, new severe epigastric pain, presyncope, or unexplained fatigue/anemia symptoms require urgent evaluation rather than refilling the NSAID.

Part 8 — Topical and Local Therapies

Topical NSAIDs, lidocaine-containing products, capsaicin, and procedure-based/local options may be useful for selected localized pain syndromes. The correct option depends on diagnosis, skin integrity, sensitivity, location, patient ability to use the product, and concurrent systemic medication burden.

“Topical” does not mean no adverse effects and does not replace evaluation of a hot joint, fracture, infection, neurologic deficit, or ischemia.

Part 9 — Skeletal Muscle Relaxants and Sedation Burden

Skeletal muscle relaxants may be considered in selected acute musculoskeletal scenarios, but they can cause sedation, dizziness, cognitive impairment, and falls. The FNP must consider age, driving, work safety, alcohol, cannabis, sleep apnea, benzodiazepines, opioids, other sedatives, and fall history.

A sedating medication can make a patient feel less aware of pain while making their risk profile worse. Define a short reassessment plan and avoid layering sedatives without a compelling indication.

Part 10 — Neuropathic-Pain Medications Require Phenotyping

Selected SNRIs, gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and topical therapies can have a role in specific neuropathic pain conditions. Medication choice depends on the pain phenotype, kidney function, mood disorder, cardiac/conduction risk, anticholinergic burden, fall risk, other sedatives, and drug interactions.

Gabapentinoids can cause dizziness and sedation and can compound respiratory-depression risk with opioids or other CNS depressants. A medication used for “nerve pain” should not be continued indefinitely without a clear diagnosis, measurable benefit, and safety review.

Part 11 — Opioids: A Benefit-Risk Decision, Not a Moral Judgment

Opioids may be appropriate for selected severe acute pain or certain other contexts, but nonopioid therapies are at least as effective for many common acute pain conditions and are preferred for subacute and chronic pain when appropriate. The goal is compassionate, individualized pain care—not abandonment, stigma, or automatic prescribing.

Before initiating opioids, establish diagnosis, expected duration, functional goal, alternatives, concurrent sedatives, substance-use history, mental-health context, pregnancy potential, organ function, prescription history as required by local law, and a plan for follow-up. Discuss realistic benefit, serious risks, storage, disposal, and what will happen when the acute indication resolves.

Part 12 — Acute Pain Opioid Principles

When opioids are clinically indicated for acute pain, choose the lowest effective exposure for the expected duration of severe pain, use an as-needed plan when appropriate, and reassess rather than allowing an acute prescription to silently become chronic therapy. Extended-release/long-acting products are not a routine starting point for opioid-naïve patients.

Do not use a single numeric threshold as a substitute for clinical judgment. Risk exists at any dose and rises with combinations, comorbidities, duration, and individual vulnerability.

Part 13 — Chronic Opioid Therapy: Reassess, Do Not Abandon

For a patient already receiving long-term opioids, do not abruptly stop or rapidly reduce therapy unless an immediate, life-threatening concern requires urgent action. Reassess benefit, function, harms, safety, and patient goals. If benefits no longer outweigh risks, optimize alternatives and collaborate on a gradual, individualized plan.

A new FNP inheriting a long-term opioid regimen should avoid reflexive continuation and avoid punitive discontinuation. Verify the diagnosis and prior plan, review prescription monitoring information as required, assess overdose risk, coordinate care, and establish a transparent follow-up plan.

Part 14 — Naloxone, Sedatives, and Overdose Prevention

Opioid overdose risk increases with benzodiazepines, alcohol, other sedatives, sleep-disordered breathing, higher exposure, kidney/liver impairment, and unexpected changes in tolerance. Naloxone education and access should be considered according to current guidance and the patient’s risk context.

Teach patients and family/support persons to recognize unresponsiveness or slowed breathing as emergencies. Medication safety includes safe storage, not sharing medications, and disposal of unused opioids.

Part 15 — Controlled-Substance Boundaries Are Clinical Safety

Follow local law, state prescription-monitoring requirements, scope rules, clinic policy, and a consistent documentation process. Boundaries should be clear and respectful: early refill requests, lost medication, dose escalation, multiple prescribers, intoxication, or concerning urine/drug-test findings require clinical assessment, not accusation.

Substance use disorder is treatable. A concerning pattern should trigger a nonjudgmental safety conversation, assessment, and referral or treatment pathway—not dismissal from care.

Part 16 — Pain in Older Adults and Patients With Multimorbidity

Older adults often have higher vulnerability to kidney injury, GI bleeding, delirium, orthostasis, sedation, falls, polypharmacy, and drug accumulation. CKD, heart failure, anticoagulation, liver disease, sleep apnea, COPD, diabetes, and depression can each change the safest option.

The best medication is often the one with the smallest expected harm that helps the patient meet a meaningful functional goal. Start with a complete medication list and a realistic follow-up plan.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: NSAID Risk in Heart Failure

A 72-year-old with HFrEF, CKD, and apixaban asks for daily ibuprofen for knee pain. They have gained 4 pounds and report ankle swelling.

Build the mechanism: NSAID exposure + vulnerable renal perfusion → sodium/water retention and possible kidney injury; anticoagulation → greater bleeding concern; new weight gain/edema → possible congestion. The FNP response is a focused safety assessment and alternative plan, not a routine NSAID refill.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: New Back Pain With Red Flags

A patient with severe back pain now has urinary retention, saddle numbness, and progressive leg weakness. They request a stronger muscle relaxant.

This is a neurologic emergency concern. New bladder dysfunction + saddle anesthesia + weakness requires urgent evaluation for possible cauda equina syndrome; medication escalation must not delay care.

Part 19 — Clinical Case: Chronic Opioid Reassessment

A patient has taken opioids for years for chronic low-back pain but reports no improved activity, increasing daytime sleepiness, and concurrent benzodiazepine use. They are fearful that the clinic will stop treatment immediately.

FNP-level care is transparent and collaborative: assess immediate safety, clarify goals and harms, review combinations and monitoring requirements, offer overdose prevention, optimize multimodal alternatives, and make an individualized plan. Avoid both unsafe automatic continuation and abrupt abandonment.

FNP Pain Medication Framework

  1. Confirm the pain syndrome and screen for emergency red flags.
  2. Set a functional goal and a time-limited reassessment plan.
  3. Use nonpharmacologic and nonopioid options when appropriate for the condition.
  4. Evaluate kidney, liver, GI, cardiovascular, bleeding, sedation, fall, and interaction risk before medication selection.
  5. If opioids are used, define indication, duration, benefit-risk monitoring, safety counseling, and exit/reassessment plan.
  6. Escalate for neurologic deficits, infection, ischemia, bleeding, severe trauma, compartment syndrome, or respiratory/CNS depression.

High-Yield Summary

Acetaminophen: check every product source and liver-risk context.
NSAIDs: can help inflammatory pain but can worsen kidney perfusion, edema, BP, heart failure, ulcers, and bleeding risk.
Topical therapy: may reduce systemic burden in selected localized pain, but it does not bypass diagnostic red flags.
Neuropathic pain: needs phenotype-guided medication selection and sedation/interaction review.
Opioids: require individualized benefit-risk assessment, functional goals, follow-up, and overdose prevention—not stigma or reflexive prescribing.
Red flags: new neurologic deficit, bladder/bowel symptoms, hot joint/fever, ischemia, severe trauma, GI bleeding, or respiratory depression require urgent care.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Pain diagnosis, controlled-substance prescribing, drug testing, prescription-monitoring review, dosing, tapering, naloxone, and referral must follow current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
